title: Efficient Scaling of LLM Training with Flexible Context Parallelism
claim: Real data have highly heterogeneous lengths, so static parallelism leaves devices idle while dynamic parallelism balances load and finishes sooner.
layout: 2 sections: stacked density plots left, static vs dynamic schematic right
description: The figure has two parts. On the left, labeled (a), are two stacked kernel-density plots. The top one shows sequence-length distributions for GitHub, CommonCrawl and Wikipedia on a log-scaled axis from 128 to 256K, with a zoomed inset on the long tail. The bottom one shows video-duration distributions for MSRVTT, InternVid and OpenVid, from 1 to 128 seconds, with a zoom inset for durations of 64s and above. Both show wide, multimodal, long-tailed spreads. On the right, labeled (b), a dashed box compares Static Parallelism with Dynamic Parallelism. Each side has stacks of 'DEV' device icons labeled '4 x', '3 x' or '2 x', next to hatched horizontal bars in pink, blue, yellow and green. In the static panel the bars have uneven lengths and the slowest sets a 4s computation time. In the dynamic panel the bars are nearly equal and the time drops to 3.5s.
caption: (a) Length distribution of text and multimodal datasets. (b) Compared to static parallelism, dynamic parallelism facilitates load balancing against heterogeneous data.
abstract: Scaling long-context capabilities is crucial for Large Language Models (LLMs). However, real-world data contain a large number of sequences with heterogeneous lengths. Existing training libraries for LLMs rely on static parallelism strategies, which suffer from severe load imbalance, redundant communication, and suboptimal hardware utilization under data heterogeneity. In this work, we propose Flexible Context Parallelism (FCP), an efficient parallelism strategy that adaptively reconfigures communication groups and context parallelism degrees during LLM training. We generalize more flexible non-power-of-two parallelism degrees and develop a polynomial-time algorithm to generate near-optimal parallelism strategies with only millisecond-level overhead per training batch. FCP is able to maintain high hardware efficiency even under extreme data heterogeneity. Experimental results demonstrate that FCP significantly outperforms Megatron-LM and DeepSpeed in both LLM and MLLM training, achieving up to 1.46x speedup in average throughput while maintaining near-linear scaling efficiency across large-scale clusters. For extremely unbalanced batches, FCP even achieves 2.24x speedup.
